programs.nl_rule:
In the input, you should see...black background with two grids of the same color and another two grid of a different color

The output grid size...is the same as the input grid size.

To make the output, you have to...copy the input grid, identify the colors of the colored grids. we will call it color A and color B. Around the grids with color A, create a 3x3 square with color B, surrounding the color A grids. Around the grids with color B, create a 3x3 square with color A, surrounding the color B grids. Now we should have four 3x3 squares, in which two squares are A color with B colored grid in their centers.

content.text:
Let me understand the rule and verifier.

Input: black background with single cells (or grids) of two colors A and B. In the example, there are 4 singletons: 9 at (3,1), 8 at (3,12), 8 at (13,1), 9 at (13,12).

So color A = 9, color B = 8. Each singleton becomes a 3x3 square: "Around the grids with color A, create a 3x3 square with color B, surrounding the color A grids." So the center stays A, and the surrounding 8 cells of the 3x3 become B. Wait, checking the output:

At position (3,1) which is 9. Output around it: rows 2-4, cols 0-2:
Row2: 8,8,8
Row3: 8,9,8
Row4: 8,8,8
Yes! So the 3x3 square surrounding a color-A cell is filled with B, center stays A.

Wait the rule says "create a 3x3 square with color B, surrounding the color A grids" - meaning the outline is B, center A.

At (3,12) cell is 8. Output around: rows 2-4, cols 11-13:
Row2: 9,9,9
Row3: 9,8,9
Row4: 9,9,9
Yes.

At (13,1) cell is 8. Output rows 12-14 cols 0-2:
9,9,9 / 9,8,9 / 9,9,9. Yes.

At (13,12) cell is 9. Output rows 12-14, cols 11-13: 8,8,8/8,9,8/8,8,8. Yes.

Then there are 5's! The verifier: after painting outbox with recolored... let me parse.

x0 = objects(I, T, F, T) : univalued objects, not diagonal, without background. So each singleton cell is an object? Actually with univalued, connectivity 4-connectivity, each isolated cell is separate object. So 4 objects.

x1 = palette(I) = {0,8,9}
x2 = mostcolor(I) = 0
x3 = remove(0, {0,8,9}) = {8,9}
x4 = lbind(other, x3): other(x3, value) returns the other value. So x4(v) = the color in {8,9} that's not v.
x5 = compose(x4, color): for object, gives the other color.
x6 = fork(recolor, x5, outbox): recolor(othercolor, outbox(object)) — creates an object where the outbox cells get the other color.
x7 = mapply(x6, x0): merge over all objects.
x19 = paint(I, x7): paint those outbox cells with the other color.

Then x8 = mapply(toindices, x0): all indices of objects = the 4 center cells.
x9 = box(x8): the bounding box outline of all 4 cells. That's a big rectangle from (3,1) to (13,12) — the outline.

Wait, box(patch) with patch = 4 cells. ulcorner = (3,1), lrcorner = (13,12). Box = outline of that rectangle.

x10 = difference(x9, x8): outline cells minus the center cells (the 4 centers aren't on the outline anyway). So the big rectangle border.

x11 = lbind(argmin, x8): argmin(x8, compfunc) — find the element of x8 minimizing compfunc.
x12 = rbind(compose, initset): compose(·, initset) → inner = initset; wait rbind(compose, initset) gives lambda f: compose(f, initset). 
x13 = lbind(rbind, manhattan): rbind(manhattan, ·)? Actually lbind(rbind, manhattan) = lambda y: rbind(manhattan, y) = fix right arg = lambda x: manhattan(x, y).
x14 = chain(x12, x13, initset): chain(h,g,f)(x) = h(g(f(x))). f=initset: x → {x}. g=x13: {x}→? hmm x13 applied to a set... 

Let me think: x14 = lambda x: x12(x13(initset(x))). initset(x) = {x}. x13({x}) = rbind(manhattan, {x}), a function: lambda y: manhattan(y, {x}). Then x12(that function) = compose(that function, initset) = lambda z: that(initset(z)) = manhattan({z}, {x}).

x15 = chain(initset, x11, x14): lambda x: initset(x11(x14(x))). x14(x) is a function; x11 = argmin(x8, compfunc) so x11(f) = argmin over x8 of f = the center nearest to x. x15(x) = {that nearest center}.

x16 = fork(manhattan, initset, x15): lambda x: manhattan(initset(x), x15(x)) = distance from x to nearest center.

x17 = compose(even, x16): whether distance is even.

x18 = sfilter(x10, x17): border cells whose distance to nearest center is even.

x20 = fill(x19, 5, x18): fill those with 5.

OK so it's complex. But for teaching, I mainly need to produce a good demonstration. Let's just show an example that I author (or transformed input).

The simplest: use show_transformed_input with the same structure as teacher example but different (or the same?). Actually if I give an input, the environment applies the gold verifier and shows the pair. That's easiest and guarantees correctness. Let me use a similar input: 4 singletons in a rectangle with colors A and B placed so that opposite corners share... wait in the example, top-left 9, top-right 8, bottom-left 8, bottom-right 9. So diagonal pairs same color. Interesting. Let's check: is that required? The rule says "two grids of the same color and another two grid of a different color." Doesn't say arrangement. But the 5 pattern depends on geometry.

Hmm, but the 5's pattern is complex. Let me figure out what the 5's do generally, because exam inputs might vary.

Let me understand: border cells of the big rectangle whose manhattan distance to the nearest center is even get colored 5.

In the example, centers at (3,1),(3,12),(13,1),(13,12). Border of rectangle rows 3..13, cols 1..12.

The 5 cells in output: row3: cols 3,5,8,10 → (3,3),(3,5),(3,8),(3,10). Let's check (3,3): distance to nearest center: center (3,1) dist 2, even → yes 5. (3,5): dist to (3,1)=4 even. (3,7): dist=6 even but output shows 5 at cols 3,5 and 8,10. Hmm (3,7): dist to (3,1) = 6 even, would be 5. But output row3: [8,9,8,5,0,5,0,0,5,0,5,9,8,9]. Columns: 0:8,1:9,2:8,3:5,4:0,5:5,6:0,7:0,8:5,9:0,10:5,11:9,12:8,13:9.

So (3,7) is 0 but (3,3),(3,5),(3,8),(3,10) are 5. Hmm (3,7): dist to (3,12) = 5, odd. dist to (3,1)=6 even. min is 5 (odd). So not 5. OK nearest center matters!

(3,8): dist to (3,12)=4 even. yes.
(3,10): dist to (3,12)=2 even. yes.
(3,3): dist to (3,1)=2 even. yes.
(3,5): dist to (3,1)=4 even. yes.
(3,7): nearest dist 5 (to (3,12)) odd. no.
(3,4): dist to (3,1)=3, to (3,12)=8; min 3 odd no.
(3,6): dist to (3,12)=6, to (3,1)=5; min 5 odd no.
(3,9): dist to (3,12)=3 odd no.
(3,11): dist to (3,12)=1 odd no.

Good.

Now, these are all border cells of the big rectangle. Also the outbox cells got painted with the other color (the 8/9 frames). Note: the big rectangle's border is NOT the same as the 3x3 frames. The 3x3 frames are drawn around each object with the other color. The 5's are then overlaid on border-of-bounding-box cells whose nearest-center distance is even.

Wait but x10 = difference(box(x8), x8). box(x8) is the outline of the bounding rectangle of the 4 centers. x8 is the 4 centers (not on the outline). So x10 = the rectangle border cells. Then fill with 5 on the even ones. This happens on top of painted image x19.

But careful: some frame cells might also be border cells and get 5. Actually 5 overwrites whatever was there.

So the full output: original black grid, plus for each singleton a 3x3 frame of the opposite color around it, plus 5's on the bounding-box border where nearest center distance even.

Hmm, this is quite specific to 4 objects. What if input has different number of objects? The exam is "held-out generator inputs" from the same generator, so likely similar structure: 4 singletons arranged in a rectangle, two of each color. The colors could vary.

Let me think about the generator. Probably places 4 single cells: colors A and B, two each, at corners of a rectangle. Then output as computed.

Let me verify the placement pattern: In example, diagonal same color. Is that determined by the generator? Possibly. But for teaching it doesn't matter much since student sees examples.

My job: teach student with demonstrations. The student is an AI learning from examples. Probably best to show several diverse examples via show_transformed_input (which auto-fills gold output). These are cheap and correct.

Let me produce a few transformed inputs with varying colors, positions, and grid sizes.

Plan: show 3-4 examples via show_transformed_input with different colors and arrangements, then maybe a query_student, then start_exam.

Let me construct inputs.

Example 1 (use varied colors): grid 16 wide, 12 tall? Let's just craft.

Actually the input convention: black background with 4 single cells (two of color A, two of color B). Let me make inputs of various sizes.

Let me design input 1:
Grid 10x10.
Place 9 at (1,1), 8 at (1,8), 8 at (8,1), 9 at (8,8). Diagonal same.
Wait need enough margin so 3x3 frames fit: at (1,1) frame needs rows 0-2, cols 0-2. OK. At (1,8) frame cols 7-9. OK. At (8,1) rows 7-9. OK. At (8,8) rows 7-9 cols 7-9. OK.

Let me use colors 2 and 4 to vary.

Input1: 10x10 all 0.
(1,1)=2, (1,8)=4, (8,1)=4, (8,8)=2.

Hmm wait diagonal pattern: top-left=2, top-right=4, bottom-left=4, bottom-right=2. Same as example pattern.

Input2: colors 1 and 3, different positions, e.g. 14 wide x 12 tall.
(2,2)=3, (2,11)=1, (9,2)=1, (9,11)=3.

Input3: colors 6 and 7, 12x12.
(3,3)=6, (3,8)=7, (8,3)=7, (8,8)=6.

Actually maybe also test whether arrangement matters (adjacent same color). But I don't know if the generator uses diagonal always. Since teacher example and likely generator use diagonal? The rule text says "two grids of the same color and another two grid of a different color" without specifying. The verifier handles any arrangement: for each object, frame colored with "other" color = the single color in palette minus mostcolor minus this object's color. Since palette has only two non-bg colors {A,B}, other(color)=the other. So regardless of arrangement.

The 5's computation depends on all 4 centers' bounding box and nearest-center distances, so arrangement matters for the 5 pattern but the verifier handles it.

For safety, I could show an example where the arrangement is non-diagonal to teach the general rule... but risk: if generator always diagonal, showing non-diagonal might confuse. Actually the student learns from examples; showing a non-diagonal example would teach the general rule which also covers diagonal. Hmm but if generator only produces diagonal, extra info is fine as long as it's consistent with the rule. Since the verifier is the rule, any input that verifies is valid. I'll mostly stick to diagonal to match, but maybe one variant.

Actually wait, is there a risk with non-diagonal like 22/44? Let me not risk. Actually the verifier works for any. Let me include one maybe.

Let me think about how many examples. The scoring is exam performance; number of show calls logged but not scored (I think). So show enough to teach. Let's show 3 examples.

Let me just be careful the input follows "input conventions" so the verifier doesn't refuse. The verifier is a function of I; it always returns something for any grid. Refusal only if input doesn't follow conventions? The verifier program verifies a transform, presumably any grid works. So fine.

Let me create examples.

Example A: 10x10, colors 2,4 as above.

Example B: 14 wide, 12 tall, colors 1,3:
Row indices 0-11, cols 0-13.
(2,2)=1, (2,11)=3, (9,2)=3, (9,11)=1.

Frames fit: (2,2): rows1-3 cols1-3 ok. (2,11): cols10-12 ok. (9,2): rows8-10 ok. (9,11) ok.

Example C: 12x12, colors 6,7, closer together maybe:
(3,3)=6, (3,8)=7, (8,3)=7, (8,8)=6. Frames: (3,3) rows2-4 cols2-4; (3,8) cols7-9; (8,3) rows7-9; (8,8) rows7-9 cols7-9. Fits.

Maybe also an example with larger gap to show 5 pattern. Example A gap: cols 1 to 8, 5's along top border between.

Let me also do a query_student to check, but queries don't give the student gold. Might be useful to see if student understands; but doesn't help student unless I show. I'll do at most one query after showing examples... actually query doesn't teach. Skip or minimal.

Better: show 3 examples, then start_exam.

Hmm, but actually could I show more examples to be safer? Logging shows number of calls but score is exam. Let me show 4 examples.

Let me produce the inputs carefully.

Actually, to maximize generalization, choose examples with varied grid sizes and colors.

Example A: 10 rows x 10 cols.

Row0: all 0
Row1: col1=2, col8=4
Row2-7: all 0
Row8: col1=4, col8=2
Row9: all 0

Wait (8,1)=4 and (8,8)=2. And (1,1)=2,(1,8)=4.

Now let me double check the verifier output for this... The environment computes it. I don't need to. Just provide input via show_transformed_input.

Example B: 12 rows x 14 cols. (2,2)=1,(2,11)=3,(9,2)=3,(9,11)=1.

Example C: 12x12. (3,3)=6,(3,8)=7,(8,3)=7,(8,8)=6.

Example D maybe with bigger separation and grid 14x14: (2,2)=5,... no can't use 5? 5 is special fill color. Avoid colors 0 and 5 maybe. Use 2 and 8? Let's use colors like 3 and 9. 

Actually the "other" color logic assumes palette has exactly 2 non-bg colors. Colors 0 (bg) and any two others. 5 is used as fill; if an input object had color 5, then palette includes 5 and other() might break. Avoid 5 as object color. Avoid 0 obviously.

Let me include D: 14x14 grid, (2,2)=3, (2,11)=9, (11,2)=9, (11,11)=3. Frames fit: (2,2) ok. (11,11) rows10-12 cols10-12 ok.

OK let's do 4 examples.

Actually maybe more useful to show examples where the two colors and positions vary to help student learn "other color". Let's go.

tools.description: Show the Student a labeled input-output pair that you authored. If your output matches the rule, the pair is shown and you receive a success acknowledgement only. If it does not match, the pair is not shown and you receive the gold output so you can correct it.
